analysis.one_liner: Requires all health care providers, drug makers, and insurers to publicly disclose their prices.
analysis.headline: The price-disclosure bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every business that sells health care to the public — hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, drug manufacturers, dentists, and insurers — to post all of their prices openly at the point of purchase and on the internet, including the discounted rates they actually accept as payment in full. Even government programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee plans would have had to disclose prices. The Health and Human Services Department could investigate and fine entities that refused to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients shopping for health care, who today often cannot find out what a service, drug, or procedure will cost them until a bill arrives weeks later. Employers and unions buying insurance for workers would also get the same price information insurers currently keep to themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying for care

how_it_helps.text: Requires hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, drug manufacturers, dentists, insurers, and even government health programs to publicly disclose all prices continuously, at the point of purchase and on the internet [S2][S3].

The disclosure must include every wholesale, retail, subsidized, and discounted price the provider accepts as payment in full — the confidential negotiated rates that drive what patients and insurers actually pay [S2][S3].

Gives the Health and Human Services Department power to investigate noncompliant entities and impose civil fines, so the disclosure requirement has teeth rather than relying on voluntary compliance [S2][S3].

Extends the requirement to government health plans themselves, including Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, so even public programs would have to publish what they pay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health care businesses — hospitals, drug companies, insurers, and provider groups — would bear the cost of compiling and publishing their full price books, and would lose the leverage that comes with secret, individually negotiated rates. Some providers would likely pass compliance costs to patients.

drawbacks.text: Posting prices alone does not guarantee lower bills: without context, a patient cannot judge whether a listed price is fair, and disclosed 'charges' often differ from what insurers actually pay, so the information may confuse more than it helps.

Compliance would be a real administrative burden, and the heaviest relative burden would fall on small physician and dental practices that would have to publish their complete fee schedules while large hospital systems absorb the same task with far bigger back offices.

The bill leaves the scope of 'health care related items, products, services, or procedures' to be defined later by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, leaving regulated entities and the public uncertain about exactly what must be disclosed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and employers, the benefit is real: price secrecy in American health care is a major reason the same procedure can cost ten times more from one provider than another, and this bill would have attacked that directly by forcing out the actual negotiated rates. The costs are compliance paperwork and the risk that raw price lists without context confuse shoppers, but those are modest next to what the disclosure could do for anyone paying a medical bill. The bill was a one-page mandate with few moving parts, which also made it easy to ignore in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three committees and sent to their health subcommittees, but none of them ever took it up, and it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Perlmutter introduced the bill on May 19, 2017, joined from the start by Rep. Mike Gallagher, making it a bipartisan introduction [S1][S3].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Government Reform — and within two weeks each had sent it to a health subcommittee [S5].

No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referral in early June 2017, and the bill expired at the end of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and drug manufacturers kept their prices secret and their negotiating leverage intact, because no committee ever acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure party lines, but the bill's small cosponsor list was bipartisan: a Democratic sponsor with 3 Republican and 2 Democratic cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish every price they accept, including the secret negotiated rates that let them charge different payers vastly different amounts for the same service. Price secrecy is central to hospital revenue leverage.

Insurers, including plan sponsors and government plan administrators, would have had to disclose what they actually pay providers — information they currently treat as proprietary. The bill targeted insurers directly in its definition of covered entities [S3].

Drug makers and pharmacies would have had to post wholesale, retail, and discounted prices publicly, exposing the spread between list prices and actual transaction prices that makes drug pricing hard for patients to evaluate.

Independent doctors and dentists would face the cost of publishing complete fee schedules, a heavier relative burden on small practices, but patients comparing prices could choose cheaper providers, which some practices would welcome.
